articles.title: Manifestantes de movimento por moradia invadem prefeitura do Recife | G1
articles.standfirst: Ato ocorreu na manhã desta quinta-feira (12). Prefeitura afirma que representantes do MLB serão recebidos por gestores para diálogo.
articles.summary: Ato ocorreu na manhã desta quinta-feira (12). Prefeitura afirma que representantes do MLB serão recebidos por gestores para diálogo.
articles.body:
Um grupo do Movimento de Luta nos Bairros, Vilas e Favelas (MLB) invadiu o prédio da sede da prefeitura do Recife , na manhã desta quinta-feira (12). Os manifestantes acessaram o hall de entrada do edifício que fica na Avenida Cais do Apolo, no Bairro do Recife, na área central da cidade.

Vídeos do momento mostram o tumulto quando mais de 20 pessoas entram pelas portas e passam pelas catracas de acesso de visitantes e funcionários. Um dos manifestantes chega a quebrar uma porta de vidro da entrada ( veja vídeo acima ).

As imagens também mostram a atuação de guardas municipais, que são confrontados ao tentar controlar o fluxo de pessoas no local. Conforme apuração da TV Globo , a chegada dos manifestantes foi por volta das 11h.

Uma foto feita logo após a invasão mostra que integrantes do movimento por moradia ocuparam o hall de entrada, por onde fica o acesso aos elevadores do prédio e a entrada da Secretaria de Finanças.

Manifestantes de movimento por moradia invadem prefeitura do Recife — Foto: Reprodução/Whatsapp

Por meio de nota, a prefeitura do Recife afirmou que o MLB "não apresenta reivindicações e diálogo há mais de um ano com a gestão municipal" . O comunicado também pontua que, durante a tentativa de invasão, os manifestantes destruíram patrimônio público.

A nota segue afirmando que a prefeitura:

"repudia quaisquer atos de violência, sobretudo contra servidores públicos municipais no exercício de funções";

"mesmo diante da postura beligerante, representantes da gestão municipal irão receber lideranças do movimento para ouvir as demandas e avaliar a viabilidade técnica e jurídica e mantêm permanente diálogo com todos os movimentos".

Segundo a prefeitura, servidores da Guarda Municipal e da Assistência Militar foram pra delegacia registrar boletim de ocorrência e relatar os prejuízos ao patrimônio público. O g1 procurou a Polícia Civil para confirmar se o caso será investigado e por meio de qual delegacia, mas não recebeu respostas até a última atualização desta reportagem.

A reportagem também tenta contato com representantes do MLB para confirmar quais são as reivindicações trazidas pelos manifestantes e se foram recebidos pela prefeitura para diálogo.

articles.title: Biggest MLB GM Meetings Takeaways to Kick Off 2026-27 MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: With a lockout expected to begin on December 2, the MLB portion of this year's Winter Meetings is expected to be canceled. That could explain why the GM Meetings were buzzier than usual.
articles.body:
With a lockout expected to begin on December 2, the MLB portion of this year's Winter Meetings is expected to be canceled. That could explain why the GM Meetings were buzzier than usual.

As one would expect under the circumstances, a general sense of uncertainty hung in the air at the Aria Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. Barring a last-minute (and highly unlikely) resolution on a new CBA, nobody knows what baseball's post-lockout economic environment is going to look like.

"The possibility of having a different economic system, you take that into consideration," said San Diego Padres president of baseball operations A.J. Preller, per Evan Drellich of The Athletic. "But it's really hard to predict what's going to happen, what the exact system is going to be or when it comes in."

Yet since rumors were flying and some deals did indeed go down, we ultimately know more about the offseason market than we did before the meetings began on Monday. That's especially true of the free-agent market.

Let's get into eight takeaways from the GM Meetings.

It Could Be a Cool Market, At Least for Relievers

The free-agent market hasn't really started moving yet, so reports of strong demand should still be taken with a grain of salt.

But in the words of one agent to Jon Heyman of the New York Post : "It's ugly."

The first major deal of the winter doesn't exactly undercut that notion. After rejecting a one-year, $10 million option to stay with the Cincinnati Reds in 2027, right-handed reliever Emilio Pagán has reportedly agreed a one-year, $11 million contract with the Detroit Tigers, pending a physical.

A single guaranteed year was less than some experts expected for Pagán. The folks at MLB Trade Rumors , for example, had the 35-year-old down for $22 million over two years.

If there's a reason for other free agents to avoid panicking, it concerns the nature of Pagán's corner of the market. The book on the free agent market as a whole is that good players are in short supply. The relief market, however, is quite strong, and thus prone to the supply outpacing the demand.

Still, if this year's market does indeed end up being a money-making dud for players, you heard it here first: Pagán was Patient Zero.

Adrian Morejon's Free Agency Is Already Surprising

Adrian Morejon has come into free agency off a terrific three-year run with the San Diego Padres, making 60-plus appearances and posting an ERA in the 2.00s each year. Per his 131 Pitching+ score, he was the top overall reliever of 2026.

Both MLB Trade Rumors and B/R's Tim Kelly project an $80 million contract for the 27-year-old lefty. That would put him among the highest-paid relievers in history, so the only way his earning power can go higher is if he decides he wants to start.

According to Will Sammon, Ken Rosenthal and Katie Woo of The Athletic, there are teams that are interested in Morejon as a starter. His preference, however, is to remain a reliever. Unless someone makes him an offer he can't refuse, that could be that as far as that storyline goes.

If that's mildly surprising, then even more surprising is the entry of the Miami Marlins into the Morejon sweepstakes. They haven't gone above $53 million for a free agent in the Bruce Sherman era, yet Kevin Barral of Fish on First reports they're interested in Morejon nonetheless.

Whether they'll end up with Morejon or even shift his market in any way remains to be seen. Either way, it's one of those things that's a little too interesting to ignore.

The Seattle Mariners Won't Be Running It Back

The Mariners were the most disappointing team in the American League this year, going from a preseason World Series forecast to just 86 wins.

It's no real surprise that they're trying to put as much distance between themselves and this season as possible. To replace Dan Wilson, they basically tabbed his personal Wario to take over the manager's chair in the person of Jason Kanzler. And now, it seems he'll have a new-look roster to play with.

With his price tag likely to fall in the $100-150 million range, Randy Arozarena has never been likely to return to Seattle. And per Adam Jude and Ryan Divish of The Seattle Times , the Mariners don't even intend to pursue him.

Then there's the surprising part: According to Jude , longtime shortstop J.P. Crawford has also been informed that the team is moving on. It's a curious choice just in the abstract, and even more so in context. The Mariners are known to be looking for a left-side infielder to pair with Colt Emerson.

The key is president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto's insistence that the Mariners get better defensively . Yet even if Arozarena (-5) and Crawford (-13) were two main offenders for a defense that finished with -58 Outs Above Average, addition by subtraction can't be the answer here.

The Chicago Cubs Have Recommitted to a Tired Bit

Tarik Skubal and the Cubs. The Cubs and Tarik Skubal. Either way, it has a nice ring to it.

It's too bad that it isn't likely to happen. According to Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic, the Cubs "appear unlikely" to pursue the two-time Cy Young Award-winning lefty.

This would seem to undercut an earlier report from ESPN's Jeff Passan about the Cubs "badly" wanting Skubal, but not necessarily. A team wanting a guy is one thing. A team being willing to pay as much as $400 million for this guy in particular? That's something else.

Despite major commitments to Alex Bregman and Dansby Swanson, the Cubs under Jed Hoyer have generally stopped short of pursuing the market's most expensive superstars. In this case, that means bypassing by far the best starting pitcher on the market even if he's the best possible fix for a rotation that ranked 28th in rWAR this year.

Per Sharma, the Cubs just aren't interested in spending like the Los Angeles Dodgers or New York Mets. And in all fairness, the Cubs did only rank…[checks notes]… third in MLB with $599 million in revenue for 2025, according to Forbes .

The Philadelphia Phillies Are Recommitting to the Only Bit They Have

If there's an anti-Cubs operation in MLB, it has to be the Phillies. If a high-priced free agent is available to help them fill a need, they're going to be interested.

And so it goes. According to Matt Gelb of The Athletic, the Phillies have "expressed interest" in the top outfielders on the market: Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki and Teruaki Sato.

You'll get no argument from us that the Phillies are a fine fit for Arozarena . Suzuki fits just as well, though that's partially because he and Arozarena are a Rorschach test for teams in need of a righty-hitting outfielder. Both are coming off their age-31 season and offer above-average bats with various hints of downside.

Sato is different. He's only 27 years old, and could thus bring valuable youth to a lineup that is just way too old. And after hitting 79 home runs in Japan across the last two seasons, he'd fit right in with the power-first vibe fueled by Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper.

Of course, Sato's defensive limitations and boom-or-bust offensive potential make him less of a fit for the Phillies. But whether it's him, Arozarena or Suzuki, they're in so deep on a free agent-fueled contention model that they might as well keep trying to throw money at their problems.

The San Diego Padres' New Owners Are Sending the Right Signals

José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones officially took control of the Padres in August, and something Jones said on August 24 still resonates.

"We are all in; it's not lip service," she said . "We are absolutely committed to this organization and we are absolutely overjoyed."

And now, here come the rumors to back it up. According to Jon Morosi of MLB Network, the Padres are interested in Tarik Skubal. Dennis Lin of The Athletic also has them in on this market's top Japan-born stars: Seiya Suzuki, Teruaki Sato and Shota Imanaga.

These names map onto the Padres' needs, which are especially prevalent in a rotation that is lacking Michael King (free agency) and Yu Darvish ( who knows? ). A bat is less of a need, but certainly a strong want. Manny Machado is not getting younger or more productive.

As for the finances, well, the Padres are already projected to spend just $4 million less in 2027 than they did in 2026. That these rumors exist tells us one of two things: Feliciano and Jones understand the value of good optics, or they really are that "all in."

The New York Mets Have Plenty of Competition for Tarik Skubal

If the Cubs were willing to put more of their ample revenue into their payroll, they'd perhaps be the favorites to land Tarik Skubal. But since they're not, all signs point toward the Mets, right?

It does seem that way, and you can take that from Jon Heyman of the New York Post as well. The Mets badly need starting pitching, and Steve Cohen's pockets go more than deep enough to afford Skubal's asking price.

They are not, however, running unopposed. According to Ronald Blum of the Associated Press, the Mets are just one of six teams set to meet with Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras.

The Padres are one. The incumbent Dodgers are another, and they may have an ace card. Katie Woo of The Athletic reported that the Dodgers prefer to re-sign Skubal on a short-term deal. It would presumably have to mimic the four-year, $240 million pact they made with Kyle Tucker, in which the shorter length is balanced against a record average annual value.

According to Heyman , the Toronto Blue Jays are also in on Skubal. Lest anyone forget their financial muscle, they spent over $700 million on Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Dylan Cease in the space of just a few months in 2025.

The New York Yankees Are Lying Low in Free Agency… For Now

As for that other New York team, things are a little weird around the Yankees right now.

There's a brain drain going on with their coaching staff, which has lost Tanner Swanson, James Rowson and Brad Ausmus to roles with other teams. And whereas Yankees fans may have been hoping for buzz on free agents like Tarik Skubal or Teruaki Sato, the most prominent name linked to the team is… Alec Bohm?

Jon Heyman of the New York Post had that report on Wednesday, with the idea being that Bohm could be a solution for a third base spot that produced only 0.2 rWAR in 2026. Bohm could either platoon with Ryan McMahon, or take over as the starter if the Yankees trade the latter.

If anything, the more notable Yankees storyline to come out of Las Vegas concerned all the defense that GM Brian Cashman had to play on Tuesday. Against criticism of the team's fundamentals. Against Jorge Posada's accusations of not feeling wanted. Against bad vibes in general, really.

Since the Yankees could have as much as $43 million to add to their 2027 payroll, this feels like a low point that won't last. As a starting point for their offseason, though, it calls the old Joe Girardi line to mind: It's not what you want.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Yordan Alvarez and PCA's MVP Wins Mark the End of MLB's Aaron Judge, Shohei Ohtani Era
articles.summary: It feels weird, doesn't it?
articles.body:
MVP announcement day has come. Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge didn't have their names called.

Pete Crow-Armstrong and Yordan Alvarez were officially named National League and American League MVPs on Thursday. They were overwhelming favorites, with FanDuel putting PCA's odds at -1500 and Alvarez's at -20000.

Crow-Armstrong went off for 45 home runs while playing Platinum Glove defense in center field. Alvarez led the majors in average, on-base percentage and slugging, while also slamming 42 homers. You can't ask for more than that from two individual players. Hence the MVP honors.

So, for the first time since 2020, neither Ohtani nor Judge is an MVP winner.

Shohei Ohtani's MVP Wins: 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025

Aaron Judge's MVP Wins: 2022, 2024, 2025

Ohtani was at least an NL MVP finalist, but even that felt dated. The four-time MVP was doing his two-way superstar thing for the Los Angeles Dodgers through June, but then knee and biceps injuries crashed the party. He last pitched on July 3. He didn't hit another home run after collecting his 30th on August 18.

Judge? He was nowhere to be seen by then, sidelined by a shoulder injury that kept him out of action between May 31 and September 8. Even after he returned, he hit the IL again just a week later with a calf strain.

For now, MLB's Ohtani-Judge era is at least temporarily over. Most likely, it will be permanent.

Shohei Ohtani's Unicorn Act Is Under Threat

The thing about doubting Ohtani is that you do so at your own peril. His whole vibe is that even if you tell him not to jump, he'll still ask, "How high?" He jumps really damn high.

Yet, there is the problem that the Dodgers were always bound to run into and finally did this year: Shohei Ohtani is human.

Without relitigating what went wrong or who should have said what and when, it's clear that 2026 is a turning point for Ohtani's career. Despite the injuries he had this year and his two elbow surgeries, he still wants to pitch. Even so, the Dodgers simply can't plan on having him pitch and hit for an entire 162-game season.

"I think it's about us putting our heads together and talking about how to start and maintain the conversations as we go," Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said in October, per Katie Woo of The Athletic . "Whether we start a little bit late — I don't know the answer to how we're going to do this, and we'll spend some time and be as thoughtful as we can about it. What that is, exactly, I don't know right now."

Ohtani's 2.68 ERA since 2021 is the best of any pitcher with at least 100 starts. His 1.79 ERA over 14 outings this year shows he can still dominate when he pitches. But if this is to be the extent of his workload, the days of his hitting and pitching being equal partners in an MVP race (as in 2022 and 2023) are over.

If so, his bat will have to carry the freight as it did in 2024 and 2025. All that took was some, well, Ohtanian standards: an OPS over 1.000 and north of 50 homers both years, plus 79 stolen bases in total.

Yet with Ohtani staring down his age-32 season in 2027, the threat of his bat having entered its post-prime years is very real. His .949 OPS and 40-homer pace before he broke down this August may be telling. If that's a hint at his new normal, expectations must adjust accordingly.

What seems for sure is that we'll never again see a 50-50 season like the one Ohtani had in 2024. Of course, it had never been done before that year. Even if he figuratively hung up his pitching arm and went back to hitting full-time, it would still be hard to turn the clock back to that magical year. You're only 29 once.

Aaron Judge Has Entered Historical Post-MVP Territory

Though he perhaps should have, as a 25-year-old in 2017, Judge didn't win an MVP before turning 30 in 2022. Then he won three in four years.

Yet even if Judge has a case (i.e., career 176 OPS+) as the greatest right-handed hitter ever, Father Time comes for everyone. This year's struggles made it two injury-marred seasons out of the last four. The New York Yankees are prepared to take precautions against further trouble.

Specifically, Yankees GM Brian Cashman made it clear during this week's GM Meetings that he foresees more time at designated hitter for Judge in the future. Here's a quote courtesy of Chris Kirschner of The Athletic :

"I'm sure he's going to need some DH time. I'm sure he doesn't want to hear that. He's an alpha. He wants to play every day… But I would think at times we'll see Judge playing DH because it's what's in his best interest, and what's in his best interest is going to be what's in our best interest, if we can just make sure that we can maintain health. He's one of the game's great players. We've got to keep those guys on the field as much as we can to get where we want to go."

In theory, more DH duty can only help keep Judge healthy and productive. But in reality, it would also make him less valuable. As an everyday outfielder, Judge has four seasons of 8+ WAR on his record. As an everyday DH, take it from Alvarez: even elite hitting from that spot only pushes WAR so far. Without any defensive value, Alvarez has twice topped out at 6.8 rWAR.

More to the point, next year will be Judge's age-35 season. The last time a hitter that age or older won an MVP award was Barry Bonds, who won annually in his age-36 through age-39 seasons from 2001 to 2004.

Before him, only two older hitters pulled off an MVP win: Mike Schmidt (36) in 1986 and Willie Stargell (39) in 1979. And that's it. The whole list.

Who Else Could Arise in a Post-Ohtani, Post-Judge MVP Landscape?

What do they say about how when one door closes, another opens?

That's what baseball could be in for if the era of Ohtani and Judge hogging the MVP awards is indeed over. It could even mark the start of a new era, like when the end of Bonds' historic 2001-04 run opened the door for Albert Pujols to win three NL MVPs from 2005 to 2009.

Because Crow-Armstrong (24) and Alvarez (29) are in their primes, they're sure to be heard from again in future MVP races. There are also contenders who have been in the running before and could be bound to luck out eventually, such as:

Bobby Witt Jr.: He's 26 and has averaged 7.8 rWAR across the last three seasons

Juan Soto: He's still just 28 and an annual lock for a .400 OBP and 30 homers

Julio Rodríguez: He's 25, a 30-30 hitter and lockdown center fielder when he's right

Elly De La Cruz: He's not yet 25, and has a 30-30 season and two 5-WAR seasons under him

Corbin Carroll: He's 26 and MLB's foremost extra-base hit and stolen base machine

Among this year's Rookie of the Year contenders, Kevin McGonigle absolutely has MVP upside. JJ Wetherholt and Carson Benge may be headed there , too. If Sal Stewart can ride home runs and RBI to a major award win, maybe guys like Pete Alonso , Junior Caminero and Nick Kurtz can, too.

It's rare for full-time pitchers to prevail in an MVP race. Lower standards for modern arms don't figure to reverse that trend. But if Cam Schlittler could be touted as an MVP candidate , then Jacob Misiorowski might one day as well. Ditto for Paul Skenes if he can get his act together.

While we're dropping names, let's go full "Screw it!" and do a wild card round: Jackson Chourio , Fernando Tatis Jr. , Jac Caglianone , Konnor Griffin , Roman Anthony .

Pick a name. Any name. Then go ahead and drop it. For the first time in a half-decade, any guess for a future MLB MVP is as good as Ohtani or Judge.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: In 2020, Christian Yelich bought a Malibu property for $5.55 million; six years later, his newly completed ocean-view home is listed for $30 million as his family looks toward Wisconsin
articles.summary: Christian Yelich has put his newly built Malibu mansion on the market for $30 million, days after the Milwaukee Brewers won their first World Series on
articles.body: Christian Yelich has put his newly built Malibu mansion on the market for $30 million, days after the Milwaukee Brewers won their first World Series on October 28. The Brewers captain bought the one-acre hillside lot in 2020 for $5.55 million, when it came with land and architectural plans but no house. Construction finished this year. His mother, Compass agent Alecia Yelich, is handling the sale, and the home’s designer says the 34-year-old plans to move his family to Wisconsin. The asking price is roughly 5.4 times what he paid.How Christian Yelich’s $5.55 million Malibu lot became a $30 million listingThe multiple looks dramatic, but it needs context. In 2020, Christian Yelich paid for a view and a set of plans. Everything after that, the foundation, the glass walls, the imported floors, the pool, came out of his own pocket, and none of those costs has been made public. So $30 million is not profit. It is an opening position for a finished product.The timing of the purchase is worth a note. That same year, Yelich was locked into a long-term Brewers contract reported at $215 million in total. He bought the lot while his baseball future was settled, then spent the next six years watching a house go up in the offseasons.The listing appeared on Realtor.com on November 4, about a week after Milwaukee beat the Tampa Bay Rays in five games. Few athletes get a bigger spotlight than that, and a seller with a headline-friendly address will notice. Whether the attention turns into a buyer at this price is a separate question.What a $30 million Malibu home actually includesThe house covers about 5,300 square feet, with four bedrooms and six bathrooms. That is modest next to some Malibu estates, so the money goes into setting and finish rather than size.Los Angeles-based KOVAC Design Studio built the home around ocean views. Floor-to-ceiling glass runs through several rooms, and the primary bedroom has glass walls that slide open to the landscape. The kitchen is a chef’s setup with marble finishes, and the heated hardwood floors were imported from France. A custom wet bar handles the entertaining.Outside, an infinity pool and a run of decks and patios give the one-acre site a resort feel. The headline room, though, is the screening room. It has an LED video wall, reclining seats and professional-grade acoustics, plus a dedicated concession room next door. A buyer at this level is paying for privacy and one uninterrupted look at the Pacific more than for square footage.Why the Yelich family is eyeing WisconsinThe reason for the sale comes from the design side. A KOVAC representative told Architectural Digest that Yelich plans to relocate his family to Wisconsin. In the reports reviewed for this piece, Yelich himself has not spoken about it, so details like timing or location in the state remain unknown.Still, the logic is easy to follow. Yelich joined the Brewers in 2018 and was named captain this year. He grew up in Southern California and went from high school in Thousand Oaks straight into professional baseball, so Malibu was always home turf. But his career now lives in Milwaukee, and a championship makes the case for putting down roots there much stronger.The sale also stays close to home. Alecia Yelich is the listing agent, and she was also the agent when her son sold his earlier Malibu house. It is a family operation, start to finish.Can Malibu deliver the asking price?Christian Yelich has been through this process before, and the history offers a useful guide. He bought a new beach house on Malibu’s Big Rock Beach in 2018 for $5.6 million. In November 2020, he listed it at $6.295 million. Then he waited. About a year later, in early 2022, it sold for $6.5 million, $200,000 above the ask.That tells you something about his approach. He is not a seller who rushes to cut. It also tells you the wait can be long, and the two homes are not comparable. A $6 million beach house draws a much bigger pool of buyers than a $30 million hillside estate. The buyer group at the top end is small, and each person in it has plenty of options.Malibu has other high-priced listings too. A separate property, the Ross Estate, hit the market the same week at $14.5 million, according to Robb Report. Even in a market where nine-figure sales make news, a $30 million ask for 5,300 square feet will draw close scrutiny from buyers and their agents.One more detail adds texture. In November 2018, wildfire forced mandatory evacuations in Malibu, and Yelich left his home there before the worst of it. He later chose to build on the hillside anyway, so the fire risk did not scare him off. A move to Wisconsin is more about where his work and family life are headed than about the place he is leaving.For now, the practical thing to watch is the first few months of the listing. His last Malibu sale took roughly a year, and any price change here will say more about the market than the asking figure does.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: New Tarik Skubal Rumors on Dodgers' Stance on Contract Talks, Meeting Schedule in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: If the Los Angeles Dodgers bring back Tarik Skubal, they hope to do so on a deal structured similarly to the one they gave Kyle Tucker last offseason.
articles.body:
If the Los Angeles Dodgers bring back Tarik Skubal, they hope to do so on a deal structured similarly to the one they gave Kyle Tucker last offseason.

Per The Athletic's Katie Woo , the Dodgers are primarily interested in retaining Skubal on a short-term contract with a high average annual salary.

The Dodgers are set to meet Skubal's camp "at some point during the next week in California," according to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic.

Tucker, arguably the best free agent available last offseason, signed a four-year, $240 million contract with LA that has opt-outs after years two and three.

The deal included $30 million in deferred money, bringing the present-day average annual value down from $60 million to $57.1 million that still set an MLB record for highest average annual salary ahead of Juan Soto's $51 million.

There are reasons to believe it might be difficult to make a short-term contract to appeal to Skubal. The first is Tucker signed his deal going into his age-29 season, so he could potentially hit the market again at 31 or 32 if he exercises his opt-out.

Skubal is going into his age-30 season and even if he were to get an opt-out after his second year, the market for a 32-year-old pitcher is not always robust.

Zack Wheeler, Framber Valdez and Jacob deGrom are currently the only pitchers making at least $30 million annually who signed their most recent contracts at the age of 32 or older.

Another potential issue for the Dodgers is Skubal is widely believed to get offers that will be the richest ever given to a pitcher by total value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds the record at $325 million over 12 years on his deal with the Dodgers.

MLB Trade Rumors predicted a nine-year, $425 million deal for Skubal.

Another factor potentially working against Skubal signing a short-term deal is he already had Tommy John surgery in college and missed time last season due to loose bodies in his elbow that required surgery.

This is Skubal's first chance to secure whatever contract he wants. His injury history, while not extensive, might lead him to take the biggest deal.

Of course, it's entirely reasonable to think Skubal enjoyed his time with the Dodgers and their history of spending to improve the roster would appeal to him that he would accept a short-term offer.

Skubal posted a 2.61 ERA with 70 strikeouts over 62 innings in 10 starts with the Dodgers after being acquired in a trade with the Detroit Tigers. He also allowed three earned runs and struck out 14 over 11 innings in two playoff starts.

articles.title: Yankees, Mets, Blue Jays Linked as Landing Spots for Free Agent Reliever in New MLB Rumors
articles.summary: Veteran relief pitcher Jonathan Loáisiga is garnering interest from multiple teams with MLB playoff aspirations in 2027.
articles.body:
Veteran relief pitcher Jonathan Loáisiga is garnering interest from multiple teams with MLB playoff aspirations in 2027.

The New York Post 's Jon Heyman reported Thursday the New York Yankees, New York Mets and Toronto Blue Jays all have the right-hander on their free agency radar.

Injuries conspired to limit Loáisiga to 50 appearances from 2023-25. Heading into the 2026 season, he settled on a one-year, $1.5 million deal from the Arizona Diamondbacks.

The 32-year-old proceeded to rebound in a big way. Across 67 innings, he struck out 48 batters and posted a 2.42 ERA and 2.88 FIP. While his strikeouts were down, he compensated by avoiding big contact.

According to Baseball Savant , Loáisiga ranked in the top 10 percentile in walk rate (5.0 percent), barrel rate (3.5 percent), and hard-hit rate (31.7 percent).

Despite his past elbow trouble, his sinker and fastball continue to hover around 97 mph. When he threw his sinker, his most frequent pitch, opposing batters slugged just .297. His five-pitch arsenal kept hitters on their toes.

Loáisiga is the No. 43 overall player on Bleacher Report's free-agent rankings this offseason.

The arm injuries will be a lingering concern for any team that signs him. Still, he stayed healthy in 2026, and his success on the mound shouldn't be a fluke.

And when Loáisiga is unlikely to command a massive contract, he's an attractive target for just about any team trying to contend.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors After 'Upbeat' Meeting with Japanese Phenom Shoki Oda amid MLB FA
articles.summary: New York Yankees officials met personally with Japanese pitcher Shoki Oda on Tuesday, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty.
articles.body:
New York Yankees officials met personally with Japanese pitcher Shoki Oda on Tuesday, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty .

Kuty reported the Yankees were "upbeat about their presentation." International scouting director Mario Garza and director of pitching Sam Briend were part of the group that attended the gathering.

Oda opted against signing with an NPB franchise and decided to make the move to the United States straight out of high school. Any team that signs the 18-year-old wouldn't expect him to be in the starting rotation on Opening Day. Instead, he'd need to work his way up through the minors.

College baseball is a possibility as well. Rintaro Sasaki enrolled at Stanford and played for two years before signing with the Miami Marlins this past summer.

MLB.com's Michael Clair and Ayako Oikawa noted Oda has a fastball that can hit the mid-to-upper 90s, and he turned heads during Japan's Summer Koshien amateur tournament.

As you'd expect, the Yankees aren't the only MLB team pursuing the young right-hander.

MLB insider Francys Romero reported the New York Mets, Philadelphia Phillies, St. Louis Cardinals, Toronto Blue Jays and Houston Astros are in the mix. Los Angeles Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes was coy when asked whether they had met with Oda.

International prospects are eligible to sign beginning on Jan. 15, but the looming labor battle could impact that timeline this winter.

articles.title: Surprise Rays Trade Considered After World Series Run, New MLB Rumors Reveal Ahead of Free Agency
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays may consider trading outfielder Jonny DeLuca this offseason, according to The Athletic's Will Sammon and Ken Rosenthal.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays may consider trading outfielder Jonny DeLuca this offseason, according to The Athletic's Will Sammon and Ken Rosenthal .

The move would be made with the intention of opening center field for right fielder Victor Mesa Jr., who enjoyed a breakout campaign as Tampa Bay made their run to the World Series this past season.

DeLuca is still under club control for three more years, but he has battled injuries throughout his career and has never had more than 370 plate appearances in a single season. The 28-year-old recorded 11 home runs and 17 stolen bases while playing solid defense at both center and right field last season, but Mesa Jr. provides the Rays with a younger option who is also a left-handed hitter.

DeLuca could draw interest in a thin market, and the Rays have promising prospects have promising prospects that could convince them to move on from him. Outfielder Jacob Melton, who was acquired in a trade with the Houston Astros last season, and star prospect Theo Gillen could both step in to provide depth.

According to The Athletic, the Rays could also trade left-handed pitcher Shane McClanahan or right-hander Ryan Pepiot. McClanahan is eligible for free agency after next season, while Pepiot is under club control for two seasons.

The Rays could be looking to operate a little differently this offseason after changing ownership and winning an American League pennant. Rays president of baseball operations Erik Neander signaled that the team would keep right-handed pitcher Drew Rasmussen, who will earn $20 million next season in his final year under club control, per MLB's Adam Berry . That would make Rasmussen the first player in franchise history to earn over $15 million in a season.

articles.title: Evan Phillips signs 3-year, $35 million deal with Braves
articles.summary: Evan Phillips pitched well in 2026 after returning from Tommy John surgery.
articles.body:
One of the best relief pitchers on the market is leaving the Los Angeles Dodgers. Veteran Evan Phillips signed a three-year, $35 million with the Atlanta Braves, the team announced Thursday.

Phillips, 32, is coming off a season in which he posted a 3.46 ERA over 26 innings with the Dodgers.

While Phillips experienced an abbreviated year, it was an encouraging performance. Phillips tossed just 5 2/3 innings in 2025 due to an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery. He returned to the majors in July and showed that his stuff had not diminished following that procedure. Phillips' fastball averaged a career-high 96.7 mph and he posted his highest strikeout rate since 2022.

He also improved as the year went on. After posting a 6.15 ERA in July, he managed a 2.61 ERA in August before dropping that to 2.16 in September and October. In the playoffs, he threw three scoreless innings for the Dodgers.

Prior to his 2025 Tommy John surgery, Phillips had established himself as one of the best relievers in baseball. From 2022 through 2024, he posted a 2.21 ERA over 179 innings. That performance made Phillips the sixth-best reliever in the sport over that period, according to fWAR. During that same period, Phillips proved himself as a closer, picking up 44 saves.

He could jump back into a closing role with the Braves. With the team's long-time closer Raisel Iglesias on the free-agent market , Phillips could be called upon to close things out in Atlanta next season. Iglesias, however, could return to the team on a short-term deal. That's exactly what the veteran did last offseason.

Even if Iglesias returns, Phillips should help. While his 2025 Tommy John surgery threatened to end that run, Phillips showed enough in 2026 to suggest his arm still has plenty left in the tank.

articles.title: Yordan Alvarez has been one of MLB's elite hitters for years. Now he finally has an MVP to solidify it
articles.summary: Alvarez has routinely been in the AL MVP conversation since he stormed into the big leagues with the Astros in 2019. He finally broke through in his eighth s...
articles.body:
Yordan Alvarez didn't really have much to prove.

The hulking Houston Astros slugger had already spent the better part of the past decade establishing himself as one of the best hitters of his generation, picking up a healthy handful of individual accolades, plus a World Series championship, along the way. But on Thursday, Alvarez collected an award that had eluded him despite his outlier offensive dominance. He was named unanimous American League Most Valuable Player , garnering all 30 first-place votes from BBWAA writers .

Famously acquired at the 2016 trade deadline for veteran reliever Josh Fields after just a few weeks as a member of the Los Angeles Dodgers organization, Alvarez is one of several main characters in the majors today — including NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and AL MVP runner-up Junior Caminero — whose professional careers briefly began elsewhere before blossoming into megastars with their second organization. The transactions that moved these players may not have seemed as consequential in the moment, but it can't be overstated the degree to which they have altered the landscape of the league in the ensuing years. And in the case of Alvarez, his ascension to greatness at the plate has been a fundamental component of this eventful and highly successful era of Astros baseball.

Though it took until his eighth big league season to claim the sport's top individual honor, Alvarez has been in the upper echelon of game-changing hitters since the day he arrived in the majors. His debut campaign was one of the most impressive partial seasons in recent memory, smashing 27 homers in 87 games with a 1.067 OPS en route to unanimous AL Rookie of the Year honors despite not getting called up from Triple-A until June 9. That fall, the 22-year-old Alvarez became the youngest American League hitter to hit a home run in the World Series since Tony Kubek in 1957, though the Astros fell to the Washington Nationals in seven games.

The 2020 season brought a potentially harrowing setback for Alvarez in the early stages of his career. He played just two games in August before needing arthroscopic surgery on both knees that rendered him unavailable for the rest of Houston's season — an ominous sequence for such a young player. He quieted those concerns quickly upon his return in 2021, leading the Astros in home runs during the regular season with 33 before earning ALCS MVP honors during Houston's run to the World Series.

The 2021 postseason run also ended in defeat in the Fall Classic at the hands of the Atlanta Braves. But in 2022, Alvarez and the Astros wouldn't be denied. In the regular season, Alvarez elevated from excellent to full-blown elite. The surface-level stats — .306/.406/.613 with 37 homers across 135 games — were extraordinary and the underlying metrics were somehow even more impressive. And come October, Alvarez bookended Houston's title run with two of the more memorable swings in recent postseason memory: the walk-off blast to stun Seattle in ALDS Game 1, and the go-ahead three-run moonshot against Philadelphia in the sixth inning of World Series Game 6 to all but clinch the championship for the Astros.

At that point, Alvarez's credentials as an offensive force of nature were unimpeachable. And yet, even that sensational season-long breakout only landed Alvarez on the podium rather than the winner's circle, as his monster campaign just so happened to coincide with two of the greatest individual seasons in baseball history courtesy of Aaron Judge, who hit 62 home runs, and Shohei Ohtani, whose two-way performance was completely unprecedented. That left Alvarez as an unusually strong bronze medalist , collecting 22 third-place votes and eight fourth-place votes on the 30 AL MVP ballots in 2022.

Alvarez's MVP quest persisted over the next two seasons, though he couldn't quite replicate his 2022-level production. He continued to cement himself alongside Judge, Ohtani and Juan Soto in the inner circle of the league's most dangerous bats — his 168 wRC+ across the 2023 and 2024 seasons ranked third behind Judge (201) and Ohtani (180) and narrowly ahead of Soto (167) — but his lack of defensive value hurt his overall case as an MVP candidate. He finished 13th in 2023 and ninth in 2024 as Ohtani and Judge added to their trophy cases.

His 2025 season unfolded in a way that invited the discouraging possibility that Alvarez's best days were behind him. He battled through a lingering right hand injury, and for the first time as a major-leaguer, his offensive output was merely good (.797 OPS) but nowhere near great. An ankle ailment ended his season in mid-September. Alvarez played in just 48 games, representing the most devastating prolonged absence in a miserable injury-ravaged Astros campaign that ultimately ended the franchise's eight-year streak of qualifying for the postseason.

Suddenly, Alvarez's place among the game's greats — and the Astros' larger role as an undisputed championship contender in the broader baseball ecosystem — both appeared threatened. Doubts began to permeate regarding Alvarez's everyday availability, especially if Houston needed to extend his defensive responsibilities considerably beyond his usual DH duties. Even more troubling was how Houston's roster was trending around Alvarez, seeming to make the Astros vulnerable to the likes of the Mariners and Rangers, who aimed to reshuffle the AL West's balance of power.

As it turned out, the divisional competition put up little resistance in 2026 despite another injury-marred and disjointed season for Houston. The Astros grinded their way to .500, a modest record but somehow one good enough to claim the division crown with the fewest wins for a full-season division winner in league history. Amid all the mediocrity, a most welcome development: Alvarez roaring back to life in spectacular fashion.

A monumental first month made it clear that Alvarez was on a mission. At the end of April, he was hitting .356/.462/.737, equating to a Ruthian 224 wRC+. His 12 homers through 32 games were tied with Judge and White Sox rookie sensation Munetaka Murakami for the most in the majors. Even as Alvarez was mashing as much as he ever had before, it looked like Judge would again be standing in his way of a push for MVP. But once Judge landed on the injured list with a rib fracture in early June — and with Ohtani established in the National League — the door was suddenly open for Alvarez to put together a signature season of his own. And that's exactly what he did.

Though a mess of a pitching staff made it difficult for the Astros to rack up wins consistently, Alvarez was a constant source of incredible production all season. He somehow came close to replicating his otherworldly opening month (1.199 OPS) with another brilliant hot streak midsummer, hitting .360/.467/.721 in July (1.188 OPS) with another nine home runs, including a walk-off blast against Tampa Bay that followed a chorus of well-deserved "M-V-P!" chants from the home crowd.

Alvarez spent the second half almost single-handedly willing Houston into postseason position, making a run at the Triple Crown in the American League while also trying to fend off Caminero in the MVP race. Pete Alonso's prolific power output headlined by his league-leading 43 homers and 113 RBI meant Alvarez had to settle for his first career batting title rather than the Triple Crown, but Caminero's relatively quiet September (.772 OPS) ensured that the MVP award would indeed finally belong to Alvarez.

The Astros' swift exit via sweep in the wild-card series courtesy of the upstart Chicago White Sox was a sobering reminder of the grander organizational questions the franchise faces as it desperately seeks to keep its competitive window open. A refresh of the leadership structure in the form of new general manager Randy Flores and new skipper Brad Ausmus is further evidence that team owner Jim Crane believed some change was necessary to get Houston back to being more of a convincing contender.

But as they push forward toward an uncertain future, the Astros can take exceptional comfort in knowing they employ one of the very few best hitters on the planet: Yordan Alvarez, AL MVP.

articles.title: Yordan Alvarez, Pete Crow-Armstrong Win AL, NL MVP 2026 Awards, Full MLB Voting Results
articles.summary: It's unanimous.
articles.body:
After putting together the best offensive season for any player in Major League Baseball, Houston Astros star Yordan Alvarez has been named the 2026 American League MVP, while a superstar-making season for Chicago Cubs outfielder Pete Crow-Armstrong has been capped off with him winning the 2026 National League MVP award.

Alvarez garnered every first-place vote and 420 total points in the BBWAA voting to beat out finalists Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays and Bobby Witt Jr. of the Kansas City Royals. Likewise, Crow-Armstrong won unanimously over fellow finalists Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Brice Turang of the Milwaukee Brewers.

Having long been established as one of the best hitters in MLB, Alvarez took his game to another level this season. The 29-year-old led MLB in all three triple-slash categories (.316/.432/.601), walks (109) and set a career-high with 42 homers.

Alvarez's 181 wRC+ was 24 points better than any other player in the league. He finished second to Witt among all AL position players in fWAR, but it was only a margin of 0.2 (7.0 to 6.8).

By FanGraphs' offensive value , Alvarez's 60.2 mark was 2.5 points better than Pete Crow-Armstrong (57.7) in second place. They were the only two players in MLB over 50.0 in the category.

Aaron Judge, Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Ronald Acuña Jr. are the only other players with at least one season worth 60.0 in offensive value since 2021.

Alvarez is only the second person ever to win MVP in either league whose primary position is designated hitter after Ohtani. The Astros slugger's previous best finish in AL MVP voting was third in 2022.

Caminero became the first Rays player to finish in the top three of AL MVP voting. He made it after hitting .276/.360/.524 and slugging 42 homers to help Tampa Bay win the AL East and reach the World Series for the third time in franchise history.

Witt has an argument as the best all-around player in the AL. He has been an AL MVP finalists twice in the last three years and finished fourth in 2025.

Alvarez is just the third Astros player to win an MVP award. He joins Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

The race between Crow-Armstrong and Ohtani appeared to shift in favor of the Cubs star over the final two months of the regular season. He was the best player in all of Major League Baseball by most metrics.

Crow-Armstrong's traditional stats were incredible with a .280/.372/.570 slash line, 45 homers and 41 stolen bases. He was the best defensive player in MLB by outs above average , fielding run value and range .

Using FanGraphs' wins above replacement as a measure of total value, Crow-Armstrong's mark of 10.6 was 3.6 wins better than the No. 2 player in MLB (Bobby Witt Jr.).

The 3.6 fWAR difference was more than the gap between Witt in second place and Rafael Devers in 50th place (3.5).

Crow-Armstrong's total fWAR was the highest in a single season since Aaron Judge's 2024 campaign (11.2).

Ohtani, who had won three straight MVP awards dating back to his final year with the Los Angeles Angels in 2023, looked like he would cruise to another win early in the season when he was dominating at the plate and on the mound.

Through July 3, Ohtani was hitting .288/.403/.524 and had a 1.79 ERA with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings.

Knee and biceps injuries prevented Ohtani from pitching again after that date. He remained in the lineup, but his slash line dipped to .232/.325/.420 in 157 plate appearances from Aug. 1 through the end of the season.

While Ohtani was trending in the wrong direction, Crow-Armstrong continued to play at an elite level and led the Cubs to a playoff berth as an NL wild card team.

Crow-Armstrong is the first Cubs player since Kris Bryant in 2016 to win NL MVP. It's the 12th time in franchise history they have had the National League MVP winner, tied with the Cincinnati Reds for fourth-most among all NL clubs.

articles.title: Caminero finishes 2nd in AL MVP voting
articles.summary: Caminero falls a few votes shy of being the MVP
articles.body:
Junior Caminero can now officially be said to have been a candidate for the Most Valuable Player as he placed 2nd among all players in the American League for the prestigious award. Yordan Alvarez received the honor as the league's Most Valuable Player for his incredible season.

It was another terrific season for Caminero in his second full year at the big league level as the now 23-year old third baseman hit .276/.360/.524 with 42 HR over 702 plate appearances, registering a 142 wRC+ and accruing 5.3 fWAR over 162 games.

Caminero possesses the fastest bat speed in the game and is among the upper echelon when it comes to xwOBA, xBA, xSLG, Avg Exit Velo, Barrel%, and Hard-Hit%. This past season, Caminero's offensive game went up a notch as he honed his plate discipline. This led to a drop in strikeout and nearly doubling his walk rate.

Since the start of the 2025 season, Caminero is second in all of baseball in homeruns (87) while he ranks 8th in wRC+ (136) and 10th in fWAR (9.9). He is the only player in franchise history to have multiple 40 homerun seasons as well. Caminero joins Eddie Matthews, Alex Rodriguez, and Juan Gonzalez as the only players to accomplish this before their age 24 season

To add to his honors this offseason, Caminero has also been named to the All-MLB First Team as the top third baseman in the game; Teammates Drew Rasmussen were named to the All-MLB Second Team as a top starting pitcher while Bryan Baker was also named to the team as a top reliever.

With his 2nd place finish, Caminero became the closest player in franchise history to be named the MVP; Evan Longoria placed 6th in 2010 and 2013.

articles.title: Mike Bianchi: Bob Boone’s death reminds us of Orlando’s baseball dream that refuses to die
articles.summary: ORLANDO, Fla. — When Bob Boone died earlier this week at age 78, baseball lost a legendary catcher, a World Series champion and one of the greatest defensive...
articles.body:
ORLANDO, Fla. — When Bob Boone died earlier this week at age 78, baseball lost a legendary catcher, a World Series champion and one of the greatest defensive players ever to squat behind home plate.

But Orlando lost something else. We lost another little piece of a big league baseball dream that has been dangling tantalizingly in front of us for nearly four decades.

Hop up on my knee and let ol' grandpappy here tell you a story about the Orlando SunRays — the Major League Baseball franchise that never was. The team that had an owner, a manager, a front office, a name and even a plan for a beautiful downtown ballpark. Everything, it seemed, except Major League Baseball's permission to exist.

And Bob Boone was supposed to be our manager.

Back in 1990, the irrepressible Pat Williams — the same visionary who helped bring the NBA's Magic to Orlando — convinced Boone to become the first manager of the would-be expansion SunRays. This wasn't some washed-up baseball lifer looking for a paycheck. Boone was a seven-time Gold Glove winner, a four-time All-Star and the catcher who helped lead the Philadelphia Phillies to their first World Series championship in 1980. He would finish his 19-year playing career having caught 2,225 major league games.

He was baseball royalty, the patriarch of a three-generation major-league family that includes his father Ray and sons Bret and Aaron, the current Yankees manager. And he believed in Orlando.

"I'm thrilled at the chance to start a franchise from scratch," Boone said back then.

Imagine that. Bob Boone standing in an Orlando dugout. Pat Williams sitting in the owner's box. A packed downtown stadium on a warm summer night. The crack of the bat. The roar of the crowd. It was all so close you could almost smell the peanuts and Cracker Jack.

Williams had recruited billionaire Amway founder Rich DeVos to bankroll the franchise. Orlando had collected 7,500 season-ticket deposits and lined up corporate commitments for thousands more. A proposed 35,000-seat ballpark was in the works.

But in 1991, baseball's expansion committee delivered the crushing verdict. Miami and Denver were in. Orlando was out. Too small a television market, they said. Too many stadium questions. Too much uncertainty.

The irony? DeVos would eventually buy the Orlando Magic later that same year, becoming the most influential owner in the city's sports history.

And Williams? He never stopped dreaming. Even after the SunRays disappeared, even after the years turned into decades, even after Orlando grew from an ambitious little tourist town into a booming American metropolis, Pat kept believing baseball belonged here.

He and co-founder Jim Schnorf launched the Orlando Dreamers in 2019, renewing the same seemingly impossible quest. Just a few days ago, Orlando climbed past Detroit into the nation's 14th-largest television market. We're still the largest American market without an MLB or NFL franchise.

And, yet, we're still considered a longshot.

Williams died in 2024. Boone is gone now, too.

Maybe that's the real legacy of these two remarkable sportsmen. Not the championships Boone won or the franchises Williams helped build, but their stubborn, beautiful refusal to accept that a dream is dead simply because somebody says no.

Somewhere up in baseball heaven, I'd like to imagine Pat Williams is working the phones, selling another impossible idea. And Bob Boone is standing beside him, catcher's mitt in hand, ready to manage.

Keep a spot in the lineup for us, gentlemen.

articles.title: Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong unanimously wins NL MVP over Shohei Ohtani
articles.summary: Crow-Armstrong posted MLB's seventh 40-40 season on offense, while being perhaps the best defensive player in baseball.
articles.body:
When it comes to hitting, baserunning and defense, no player in MLB came close to matching Pete Crow-Armstrong in all three this season. He received some deserved hardware for that Thursday.

The Chicago Cubs outfielder won the 2026 National League MVP Award over finalists Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Brice Turang of the Milwaukee Brewers. He is the first Cub to receive the honor since Kris Bryant in 2016.

The vote was unanimous, with Crow-Armstrong receiving all 30 first-place votes from the BBWAA. It's the 11th time in NL history that has happened with MVP, and the fourth consecutive year after Ronald Acuña Jr. in 2023 and Ohtani in 2024 and 2025.

Ohtani received 26 second-place awards, with Turang, Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski and Philadelphia Phillies slugger Kyle Schwarber responsible for the other four.

On the American League side, Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros won MVP unanimously after a historic season on offense . It is the third time in the past four years that both MVPs have been unanimous, joining 2023 (Ohtani and Acuña) and 2024 (Ohtani and Aaron Judge).

Before 2023, it had never happened in the history of the BBWAA MVP awards, which go back to 1931. This is also the first time in MLB history that both MVP and both Cy Young Awards were unanimous.

By the end of the season, Crow-Armstrong's case for MVP was overwhelming. If it had to be boiled down to a single sentence, it would probably be something like "A player just posted the seventh 40-homer, 40-stolen base season in MLB history , while also delivering arguably more defensive value than any player in the league."

Crow-Armstrong's 45 homers and 41 stolen bases got him into the 40-40 club populated by Jose Canseco, Barry Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, Alfonso Soriano, Acuña and Ohtani. He was the best hitter in the NL overall this season, leading the league in homers (45), runs (119), slugging percentage (.570), OPS (.943) and total bases (357).

On the defensive side, he won his second straight Gold Glove in center field and led all of MLB in Statcast's Fielding Run Value at 26 . Both the eye test and the advanced stats were in agreement: his glove alone was a force this season.

Not only was Crow-Armstrong the clear MVP, he also won the Hank Aaron Award as the NL's top hitter and the Platinum Glove as the NL's top fielder. No other player has done that since the Platinum Glove was introduced in 2011.

Pete Crow-Armstrong ran away with MVP in the second half

As clear as the decision was by October, it took months for Crow-Armstrong to be considered the favorite. Ohtani was in pursuit of a fifth career MVP award, the most in MLB history outside of Bonds, and seemed likely to win it as late as July thanks to his immense value as both a designated hitter and starting pitcher.

Crow-Armstrong also struggled early in the year, ending May slashing 237/.325/.388 at the plate.

However, Ohtani stopped pitching in early July due to a knee issue that led to a lubricating injection over the All-Star break. As his return to the mound kept getting pushed back (all the way to 2027, eventually), the Dodgers star became just a hitter, and Crow-Armstrong more than matched him on that front, slashing 302/.397/.668 after May thanks to a midseason swing adjustment.

Three of Ohtani's four MVP awards have been built on his value as a two-way player. He was an elite hitter in each season, and even a limited number of good innings as a pitcher are usually more valuable than what most position players can deliver on defense. Crow-Armstrong's glove, however, was another animal.

The comparison can be boiled down to two combinations of stats, using the Baseball Reference calculation of wins above replacement (WAR). No. 1:

a hitter with a .275/.377/.512 slash line and 11 stolen bases in 618 plate appearances (3.2 WAR)

a pitcher with a 1.79 ERA in 85 2/3 innings (3.2 WAR)

a hitter with a .280/.372/.570 slash line and 41 stolen bases in 726 plate appearances (8.3 WAR)

162 games of the best defensive center fielder in baseball (2.1 WAR)

Voters overwhelmingly chose No. 2, which also came with the benefit of late-season momentum. By September, knee, neck and biceps issues were affecting Ohtani's hitting as well, so the Dodgers placed him on the IL. That was effectively the end of the race.

The Cubs went on to lose in the NL wild-card round, falling in two games to the San Diego Padres with Crow-Armstrong going 0-for-7 with a walk and four strikeouts. That didn't affect the MVP voting, as all award votes are cast at the end of the regular season.

As disappointing as the ending was, the 2026 season was ultimately a triumph for Crow-Armstrong. The New York Mets selected him 19th overall out of high school in the 2020 MLB Draft, then traded him to the Cubs a year later in a Javier Báez deal that now ranks among the most regrettable for any team in recent memory.

Crow-Armstrong reached the majors in 2023, became a full-time starter in 2024, an All-Star and Gold Glover in 2025 and, finally, an MVP in 2026. His career has been a steady but steep rise into the highest tier of MLB superstars, and he may only be getting started at 24 years old.

articles.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong's 'quantum leap' landed an unlikely MVP campaign
articles.summary: PCA's magical 2026 season was impressive enough to beat out Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani for the NL's top award.
articles.body:
A player's development is rarely linear in baseball. After taking several steps forward, it's not unusual to see someone move one or two steps backward. Coming into the 2026 season, the Chicago Cubs were waiting to see which direction Pete Crow-Armstrong headed.

Nearly eight months later, the superstar center fielder showed the baseball world that his struggles were minor hurdles en route to becoming one of the best players in the sport.

Crow-Armstrong was named National League MVP on Thursday night , making him the youngest player to win the award (24) since Cody Bellinger (23) won the NL MVP in 2019. PCA received all 30 first-place votes , beating four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani, who had won the award in 2024 and '25, and Milwaukee Brewers star Brice Turang.

"I want to be better than I was the day before and really that's been all that I've needed to motivate myself with for as long as I can remember," PCA said on the MLB Network broadcast after winning the award. "I've had really important people that wake me up every day."

Being named the 2026 NL MVP is the cherry on top in a season full of deserved accolades for Crow-Armstrong. What made this season, in which he became the seventh player in MLB history to join the 40-40 club, even more special was that his dominance shined with his bat and glove. Crow-Armstrong won his second Gold Glove Award and was honored with the NL's Platinum Glove Award as the best defender in the league.

What makes PCA's 2026 season so remarkable is the turnaround it took to make it happen.

Crow-Armstrong's second half in '25 in which he carried a .634 OPS was one to forget, but the 2026 NL MVP knew he had to come into the season with a new offensive plan. And after signing a six-year, $115 million deal right before the season began, the pressure was on to show he could be the star the Cubs hoped he would be.

The first six weeks of the season, it looked like the player who ended 2025 had returned and it would be more of the same. But Crow-Armstrong quickly showed he was not only a different player, but the NL's best player. From May 1 until the end of the regular season, he became must-see TV as his highlight-reel defense in center field, tape-measure homers and electric speed captivated baseball.

Crow-Armstrong finished the season hitting .280 with an NL-leading 45 homers (tied with the Phillies' Kyle Schwarber), 31 doubles, eight triples and 41 stolen bases. He also led the NL with a .942 OPS.

"Watching the consistency of the at-bats, that's been an amazing transformation," Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said in September. "I think a lot of coaches deserve a lot of credit, and [Pete] deserves the lion's share of the credit for sticking with it. And just his decision-making in the box.

"I've never seen a player develop at this rate. This is a quantum leap in terms of his decision-making. I mean, the higher OPS against the lefties — he's had some at-bats against great lefty relievers. He's laying off pitches just a little bit outside. That was unimaginable one year ago."

He also became the second left-handed hitter in franchise history to hit 40 or more homers and the first Cub to win MVP since Kris Bryant in 2016.

But to be the best, you have to beat the best, and when you play in the same league as Ohtani, that is no small feat. Yet Crow-Armstrong did something many believed was impossible. And after months throwing haymakers with Ohtani in the NL MVP race and jockeying for position, it was a scorching August that pushed Crow-Armstrong in the lead for good.

Crow-Armstrong hit an eye-popping 14 homers in the month, carrying an incredible 1.069 OPS to pull away from the Dodgers' superstar, who missed some time late in the season with various injuries. It's no surprise that PCA's MVP moment came on Aug. 29 as he slugged three homers against the Cincinnati Reds with another former Cubs MVP, Sammy Sosa, in attendance.

Crow-Armstrong's season won't be forgotten in Chicago and his turnaround is one the Cubs as an organization should be proud of. After years searching for their next superstar, PCA has shown he'll be the guy who carries the franchise for years to come with three letters …

articles.title: Rangers Eye Sato But Phillies Could Land Power Hitter First
articles.summary: The Rangers are interested in Teruaki Sato, but his high price tag makes a deal unlikely. Philadelphia could step in for a left-handed slugger with massive p...
articles.body:
The Texas Rangers are showing interest in Japanese star Teruaki Sato, but a deal there looks like a long shot. According to Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic, the club is just one of several teams watching the market. The Phillies are also among the suitors, which puts Philadelphia in a prime spot to make a move if the price stays reasonable. This year's free agent class likely features Sato as the premier position player, and his power bat might solve a lineup requiring more punch.

Texas has bigger financial headaches than a new outfielder right now. The club is focused on shedding obligations to stars like Corey Seager, Jacob deGrom, and Nathan Eovaldi. MLB Trade Rumors predicted Sato would sign a five-year, $80 million deal, but other public estimates put the value well into the nine-figure range. The signing team also has to pay a posting fee based on that contract value. With the Rangers ending the 2026 season with a $218.7 million luxury tax number, spending big on Sato seems unlikely given their current payroll constraints.

This year, Sato has hit 39 home runs for the Hashin Tigers, generating immense power from the left side. Across 614 plate appearances, he followed that performance with a .306/.383/.609 slash line. However, evaluators have questions about his pure hitting ability against better pitching. In a league where pitcher quality falls below Major League Baseball standards, he struck out at a 26.7 percent rate. Sato has a decent chance of punching out 30 percent of the time in the big leagues. Teams might accept those whiffs if he keeps hitting 30 or more homers, but it is a risky bet.

While Sato has primarily played third base in Japan, numerous scouts believe he is better suited for a corner outfield role in the majors. Josh Jung secures the hot corner for Texas, but the team faces a vacancy at designated hitter as Joc Pederson explores free agency. They could also sign a left fielder while designating Wyatt Langford as the everyday center fielder. The Phillies need a left-handed bat to balance their lineup, and Sato fits that need perfectly. If the Rangers pull back due to cost, Philadelphia could swoop in to grab a player who hit 40 homers just one season ago.

An estimated $192.8 million cash payroll and a $218.7 million luxury tax number marked the end of the 2026 season for the Rangers.

articles.title: Ranking Tarik Skubal's Landing Spots With Mystery Team Predictions Amid Latest Free Agent Rumors
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal is the biggest name on the 2026-27 MLB free-agent market, and with a potential lockout looming, there have been considerable rumblings surrounding his market in recent days.
articles.body:
Tarik Skubal is the biggest name on the 2026-27 MLB free-agent market, and with a potential lockout looming, there have been considerable rumblings surrounding his market in recent days.

Ronald Blum of the Associated Press reported on Tuesday that Skubal is planning to meet with six teams in the coming weeks, with the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets and San Diego Padres part of that group.

On Wednesday, MLB insider Jon Heyman reported that the Toronto Blue Jays are also part of that group, leaving two mystery teams in the mix if this is indeed the list of finalists.

Ahead, we have speculated on the most likely mystery teams, along with ranking the four confirmed suitors by their likelihood of signing the two-time Cy Young winner.

1. San Francisco Giants: There is a clear need for another frontline starter alongside Logan Webb, and the Giants have enough money tied up in veteran bats that they should be in win-now mode even after a 97-loss season.

2. Baltimore Orioles: After making a splash with the Pete Alonso signing last winter, nothing would move the needle more for the Orioles than finding a bona fide ace, especially with Trevor Rogers on the free-agent market.

3. Atlanta Braves: A stagnant contender in need of a roster shakeup rather than a full-scale retooling, the Braves could build a lethal one-two punch with Skubal and Chris Sale. Their pursuit would also potentially block interested division rivals in the Mets and Phillies.

4. Philadelphia Phillies: With Zack Wheeler coming off the books after the 2027 season, Skubal could fill his spot on the staff and on the payroll. However, holes at third base, in the corner outfield and at the back of the bullpen represent more pressing needs.

5. Chicago White Sox: There may be no team where Skubal fits the "missing piece" profile more than the White Sox, who are fresh off a dramatic turnaround from 102 losses to a postseason berth. They have a dynamic young offensive core, but their starters ranked dead last in innings pitched, and Sean Burke is projected as the 2027 staff ace.

6. Arizona Diamondbacks: No one saw the D-backs coming when they signed Zack Greinke (6/$206.5M) or Corbin Burnes (6/$210M), so it would be wise not to completely overlook the D-backs in this market.

7. Washington Nationals: The Nationals are essentially White Sox Lite in this discussion, as their offensive core is similarly further along than the pitching staff in their rebuilding efforts and they theoretically have money to spend. The 77-85 finish is a tougher sell, though.

Despite needing to rebuild essentially their entire starting rotation, the Cubs are not expected to enter the Skubal sweepstakes, according to Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic.

These teams have the hypothetical spending power, but the starting rotation is not their most pressing need this offseason: Mariners , Red Sox , Yankees

These teams are unlikely to spend at the level it would require to sign Skubal, are more focused on retooling the roster or are not competitive enough to be an attractive landing spot: Angels , Astros , Athletics , Brewers , Cardinals , Guardians , Marlins , Pirates , Rangers , Rays , Reds , Rockies , Royals , Tigers , Twins .

RHP Dylan Cease RHP José Soriano RHP Trey Yesavage RHP Cody Ponce RHP Spencer Arrighetti

The Blue Jays already swung a blockbuster deal to acquire José Soriano from the Angels at the trade deadline, while also buying low on Spencer Arrighetti in the trade that sent Daulton Varsho to the Astros.

Those moves will potentially help stabilize the starting staff, but they could still benefit greatly from another frontline arm alongside Dylan Cease while Trey Yesavage continues to develop.

They have circled some major free agents in recent years, including Shohei Ohtani, so their viability as a suitor is real. The question is whether they would be willing to go all-in on Skubal when they are also known to be aggressively pursuing a corner outfield bat.

With ace Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Walker Buehler and trade-deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize now free agents, the Padres' starting staff needs to be rebuilt.

They also stand to lose a pair of key bullpen arms in Adrián Morejón and Jason Adam, which will put more pressure on a rotation that ranked 27th in the majors in innings pitched in 2026.

There is a lot of long-term money on the books with Manny Machado, Fernando Tatis Jr., Xander Bogaerts and Jackson Merrill all under contract through at least 2033, which could give them pause if the league is indeed headed for a salary cap.

However, they need to do something to address the void in the rotation, and Skubal is the type of needle-moving splash that could bridge the gap to the rival Dodgers in the NL West.

RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto LHP Blake Snell RHP Tyler Glasnow RHP Roki Sasaki RHP Emmet Sheehan

The Dodgers have plenty of high-profile talent in their starting rotation mix, but Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Shohei Ohtani all come with significant injury question marks, and that's a big reason why the Dodgers traded for Skubal at the deadline.

Those concerns are still a central piece of the puzzle as they look to rebound from getting swept by the Brewers in the NLCS, but the potential salary cap stands to impact the Dodgers more than any team in the sport given all the money they already have on the books. That could mean another long-term mega-deal is simply not in the cards.

"According to several team sources, the Dodgers' interest in a return hinges on Skubal accepting a shorter offer than he'll likely receive from other bidders," wrote Kate Woo of The Athletic .

That does not by any means remove the Dodgers from the running, and last year's Kyle Tucker deal proved a high AAV can edge out a longer commitment. If Skubal prefers a clear path to World Series contention over more guaranteed money and a cloudier contention outlook, the Dodgers might still belong in the No. 1 spot.

RHP Nolan McLean RHP Christian Scott LHP Zac Thornton RHP Kodai Senga LHP Sean Manaea

With Freddy Peralta, Clay Holmes and David Peterson all gone from last year's Opening Day rotation, the Mets will be looking to add multiple arms alongside the promising young trio of Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton.

They were not afraid to hand record-setting AAV deals to Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander in the early days of the Steve Cohen era, and there is no indication the front office will stop throwing money at the contention problem this winter.

In terms of sheer spending power and roster need, there is no more obvious landing spot for Skubal on a record-setting, long-term deal.

The question is whether Skubal believes this Mets team can be a World Series contender during his remaining prime, and if that's a top priority in picking his landing spot, the front office will need to convince him they have a legitimate direction rather than just deep pockets.

articles.title: Latest Tarik Skubal Rumors on 'Industry Favorites' to Land Star amid Mets, Dodgers Links
articles.summary: The New York Mets could be poised to hand out another historic contract in free agency as they look to rebound following their disappointing 74-88 record in 2026.
articles.body:
The New York Mets could be poised to hand out another historic contract in free agency as they look to rebound following their disappointing 74-88 record in 2026.

Per ESPN's Jorge Castillo, Alden Gonzalez and Jesse Rogers , the Mets are viewed as "industry favorites" to sign Tarik Skubal with the two sides set to meet next week.

The Los Angeles Dodgers remain interested in bringing back Skubal, though they reportedly prefer to do a short-term deal with a high average annual salary similar in structure to the four-year, $240 million contract Kyle Tucker signed last offseason.

Most predictions have Skubal signing the richest deal ever for a pitcher. MLB Trade Rumors , for instance, is projecting a nine-year, $425 million contract for the 29-year-old.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract with the Dodgers is currently the high-water mark for a starting pitcher. Gerrit Cole (nine years, $324 million) is the only other pitcher with a contract worth at least $300 million.

Mets owner Steve Cohen has not shied away from spending on marquee players. Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor are two of the eight highest-paid position players in MLB. Soto's $765 million deal is the richest in the history of North American pro sports.

Skubal and his representatives are believed to have meetings set up with at least six teams right now, including the Mets, Dodgers and San Diego Padres. The Toronto Blue Jays are also said to have interest in the two-time AL Cy Young winner, as well as two mystery teams.

One team that appears to have been ruled out on Skubal is the Chicago Cubs. Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic reported on Monday the Cubs are "unlikely" to enter the bidding for the star pitcher, despite their need for help on the mound.

Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns told reporters at the general managers' meetings this week there is "no question" they will add to their rotation this offseason, though he noted they are looking at various way to do so:

"We have a lot of confidence in the arms we have in-house and a good segment of that group showed over the second half of the year that they can compete at a high level in the major leagues. We're going to add to that group. There is no question we're going to add to that group. I firmly believe we have got some really talented arms that can pitch at the top of the rotation."

Nolan McLean, Sean Manaea and Christian Scott are the only Mets pitchers currently under contract who threw at least 100 innings for the team in 2026. McLean and Scott were the only ones to make at least 20 starts last season.

Skubal posted a 2.72 ERA with 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings across 26 starts between the Dodgers and Detroit Tigers last season.
