articles.title: The 2027 Lockout Preview – Overview
articles.summary: The 2026 season may not have been great for fans of the Toronto Blue Jays, but for baseball in general, it was a stellar year. While the books aren’t entirel...
articles.body:
The 2026 season may not have been great for fans of the Toronto Blue Jays, but for baseball in general, it was a stellar year. While the books aren't entirely opaque, direct revenue raised by the MLB is estimated at over $13B for the season, the highest ever, and continuing a steady trend line since the COVID shortened 2020 season of about 4-7% growth year over year. Three teams changed ownership this year – Tampa Bay, San Diego, and Los Angeles – selling for $1.7B, $3.9B, and $4B respectively, despite all three facing challenges ranging from the need for a new stadium, a small media market, and a complete overhaul after decades of irrelevance. And yet, despite all of this success, owners are expected to lock out the players on the final minute of December 1 st , 2026.

Why would a business that is experiencing runaway success risk everything with the potential loss of games and revenue in 2027? How will the players respond? How certain are we that we're going to see one side or the other fold and what is at sake for the future? This series will hopefully shed some light on what is often a confusing and opaque process before events start to unfold in real time. Or explain things you already know but give you a dedicated comment section to rail against the players/owners/system/TheMan.

This whole process revolves around the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) between the MLB and the MLBPA. The CBA remains in force for five years and must be renegotiated after that time. The current CBA expires on Tuesday, December 1 st at 11:59PM which is why the expectation of when the lockout will begin is so precise. The CBA is a wide-ranging agreement which covers extremely consequential things like arbitration, free agency requirements, roster size as well as significantly less important elements like a mandatory chef in each clubhouse. Negotiations for the owners are headed by the MLB Deputy Commissioner Dan Halem and his team and the players are represented by MLBPA Executive Director Bruce Meyer and his team. Halem and MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred communicates with the 30 MLB owners and their specific representatives, and Meyer meets with the Executive Subcommittee and the 30 Team Player Representatives. In order to reach a decision, the owners need a 75% majority of votes, so 23 out of 30 owners. The players in theory only need a straight majority out of the 38 votes from the Executive Subcommittee and the Team Player Representatives. For example, in the last CBA negotiations in 2022, the 8 man Executive Subcommittee voted unanimously to reject the owners offer but lost the full vote by the Representatives 26-12.

The terms are often used interchangeably and are both forms of work stoppages but there is a significant difference between the two. Strikes are player led work stoppages during which the players withhold their services. The last MLBPA led strike took place in 1994, specifically to block the implementation of a salary cap, which cancelled the rest of the season and post season and lasted until April 2, 1995. Lockouts are initiated by the owners, which means all player related activities and communications are halted, including trades, signings, training and access to team facilities until the lockout is lifted. The reasoning behind a lockout is that having hard deadlines provides teams leverage in the negotiations, as players will be pressured by not having contracts, job security or access for training and rehab resources to accept a contract more favourable to the owners.

Both sides have been preparing for a potential lockout for the last several years. A series of proposals have gone back and forth between the MLB and the MLBPA, mostly for the sake of media coverage and positioning, as each group looks to bring the public on their side. While the details can shift rapidly, each has outlined a broad agenda of their priorities.

Salary Cap and Floor: Tied as a baseline requirement to all league proposals, MLB has proposed a hard salary cap of roughly $258.2 million and a salary floor of $180.2 million, paired with a 50/50 revenue split between owners and players to be implemented in 2028.

Shorter Regular Season and Expended Playoffs: Reducing the regular season from 162 to 154 games starting in 2029 to provide a standard weekly off-day and a dedicated Monday broadcast window. Extending the Division Series to best-of-seven and allowing higher-seeded teams to pick their opponents.

Roster & Offseason Changes: Weekly roster-setting windows, a 14-pitcher limit, Rule 5 draft adjustments, a reduced draft of 12 rounds excluding high school players, an international draft and an offseason transaction calendar featuring a winter quiet/frozen period.

Free Agency and Wages: Increasing the minimum salary to $1M and decreasing the service time requirements from 6 to 5 years before qualifying for free agency.

The key for the owners is that they are willing to offer all kinds of incentives for the players; things that are good for them like a year less of team control, having a day off every week built into the calendar, making it more likely good teams have deeper playoff runs, and increasing their potential post season earnings. However, the two red lights for the players are the glaring blaring siren of a salary cap, and the reduction in the draft allowing them to further shrink their farm systems without losing competitive balance with other teams.

Tax on Low-Spending Teams: A "competitive-integrity tax" targeting low-spending clubs (mirroring the luxury tax for high spenders).

Higher Thresholds & Salaries: Raising the base Competitive Balance Tax (CBT) threshold to $300 million (up from $244 million), near-doubling player minimum salaries, and increasing local television revenue sharing. Also Expanding active rosters from 26 to 28 players for the first 15 days of the season.

Reduced Service Time: allowing players over thirty to reach FA after 5 years.

The key for the players is challenging the disparity in team payrolls in a way that doesn't limit player earning potentials that a cap would, while expanding financial opportunities for younger players and players who earn MLB spots later in their careers. While the players proposal is more of a wish list, it is wrapped around one absolutely unshakable point, which is that the MLBPA will not consider a salary cap under any circumstances. While the Commissioner and his office have been trying to sell the cap and floor to the players by pointing out the proposed cap and floor would cost 8 teams about $580M in payroll, but it would compel 12 teams to raise their payrolls a little over $615M.

While things will develop very quickly, the starting positions by both sides couldn't be further apart. It also isn't helped by the complete lack of trust in the MLB owners by the MLBPA. They have resisted every effort for any kind of consistent transparency in their revenue or financial situations, so the MLBPA rejects the owners position that small market teams are uncompetitive and there's no other mechanism but a cap to re-establish parity. As Paul Beeston famously said: "Anyone who quotes profits of a baseball club is missing the point. Under generally accepted accounting principles, I can turn a $4 million profit into a $2 million loss, and I can get every national accounting firm to agree with me." Even if the cap is tied directly to a 50/50 revenue split, there is absolutely no doubt by the players the ownership will contort itself every which way possible financially to separate various lines of business out as baseball revenue to reduce that number.

So in this environment of strong distrust, a game where payrolls for some have exploded and for others receded amidst record revenue and franchise values and truly eyepopping contracts handed out to star players, is there a way to find common ground without losing games, is there an avenue for both sides to step down and kick the bigger issues down the road another five years, or is this finally time for the all out war over a salary cap that has been brewing for over fifty years?

articles.title: Assessing Evan Phillips’ Singing With The Atlanta Braves
articles.summary: The Atlanta Braves signed Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million contract, bolstering one of the best bullpens in MLB. Phillips will become a high-levera...
articles.body:
The Atlanta Braves signed Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million contract , bolstering one of the best bullpens in MLB.

Phillips will become a high-leverage arm for the Braves in the back end of the bullpen. While he's a huge addition on his own, the Phillips signing raises other questions Atlanta needs to answer.

Phillips has battled injuries and has only thrown 31.2 innings across 38 appearances over the past two seasons . However, when he has pitched, Phillips has been effective. Since 2025, he has a 2.84 ERA (151 ERA+) and 39 strikeouts to just eight total walks.

If he can stay healthy, Phillips will become a major addition to the bullpen. His addition provides a clearer vision for other offseason moves, particularly with pitching.

The Phillips Signing May Be Atlanta's Way of Moving On From Iglesias

Iglesias has been the Braves' closer over the past two seasons. Iglesias is a free agent, and the Phillips signing may signal Atlanta is moving on. Last offseason, the Braves inked a three-year deal with Robert Suarez, who closed for the San Diego Padres. Suarez didn't close during his first season in Atlanta, but he could step back into that role.

The Braves closer finished fifth in NL Reliever of the Year voting, including two third-place votes. Iglesias was an NL All-Star this season, posting a 2.55 ERA and 34 saves in 37 opportunities. At 36, Iglesias is getting older, but he's still effective. Phillips' signing doesn't rule out the possibility of Iglesias returning, as the Braves may have other plans for one of their current bullpen arms.

Fuentes Is Heading Back to the Rotation and Phillips Fills His Bullpen Spot

Didier Fuentes rose through Atlanta's minor league system as a starting pitcher. When he debuted in 2025, that was the role he played. All four of his big-league appearances last season were starts. This season, things changed as Fuentes spent most of the season out of the bullpen. It was a success, as Fuentes posted a 2.45 ERA and 92 strikeouts in 73.1 innings pitched.

While he was great out of the bullpen, the Braves want him to be a starter once again. The plan is for him to join the rotation in 2027. Regardless of what transpires, Atlanta has ensured that they have one of the top bullpens in MLB next season and beyond. There are other holes on the roster, but the bullpen should be a strength for the Braves in 2027.

Atlanta gets the offseason started with a key bullpen addition. What they do between now and Dec. 1 will be critical, as they need to figure their roster out before a potential lockout.

The future of baseball is uncertain, but the Braves are setting themselves up to still be among the best in baseball moving forward.

articles.title: Jake Bauers, Red Sox Reportedly Agree to Contract After World Series Run, New MLB Rumors on Deal
articles.summary: A breakout 2026 season for Jake Bauers has resulted in a new contract from the Boston Red Sox in free agency.
articles.body:
A breakout 2026 season for Jake Bauers has resulted in a new contract from the Boston Red Sox in free agency.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , Bauers has agreed to a four-year, $58 million deal with the Red Sox.

After being a backup journeyman outfielder early in his career, Bauers found his footing as a 29-year-old with the Milwaukee Brewers during the 2025 season. He hit .235/.353/.399 in 85 games.

The 2026 campaign saw Bauers maintain that patient approach at the plate and add power to his game. He finished with a .266/.389/.484 slash line and 26 homers in 144 games during the regular season.

Bauers' 143 wRC+ ranked seventh among all qualified hitters. He ranked third in on-base percentage, behind Yordan Alvarez (.432) and TJ Rumfield (.390).

During the Brewers' postseason run to the World Series, Bauers became a household name thanks in large part to two plate appearances in the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The first was a 12-pitch walk against Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 that drove his pitch count up, resulting in the shortest playoff start of his career (2.2 innings). The second was an 11-pitch at-bat against Blake Snell in Game 3 that ended with a two-run homer to put Milwaukee up 3-2.

Bauers was named NLCS MVP thanks to a .286/.412/.571 slash line in the Brewers' four-game sweep to help them clinch their first World Series appearance since 1982.

Prior to joining the Brewers after the 2023 season, Bauers had bounced around with multiple teams as a fourth outfielder. He was originally drafted by the San Diego Padres in 2013, was traded to the Tampa Bay Rays after the 2014 season.

After making his MLB debut with the Rays in 2018, Bauers was traded to the Cleveland Guardians in December 2018. He played 117 games in 2019, didn't appear in a game during the 2020 season and was traded to the Seattle Mariners midway through the 2021 campaign.

Bauers split time in the minors with the Triple-A affiliates for the Cincinnati Reds and New York Yankees in 2022. He made it back to the big leagues in 2023, appearing in 84 games with the Yankees.

This past season, his final year of arbitration, Bauers made just $2.7 million from the Brewers. He turned out to be one of the best bargains in the sport and figures to hold a lot of value going forward with his bat-to-ball skills.

As long as the power that showed up in 2026 remains part of his game, Bauers will be a huge addition for a Red Sox team that struggled to hit down the stretch and in their brief playoff run that ended in a two-game sweep against the New York Yankees in the AL Wild Card round.

Bauers' signing is going to further speculation that a trade involving Jarren Duran could be on the horizon. The Red Sox were already crowded between first base and the two corner outfield spots.

Willson Contreras is locked in as the starter at first coming off an All-Star season. Wilyer Abreu had a breakout 2026 after being a solid starter in each of the previous two years. Roman Anthony, as long as he is healthy, might be the best hitter on the team.

That leaves at least one of Duran of Masataka Yoshida, both of whom have already been mentioned as trade candidates, potentially pushed out with Bauers coming in.

Regardless of the next moves from Boston, Bauers is a huge addition for the lineup because of his approach and ability to get on base. As long as the power he displayed last season continues going forward, this could be a bargain deal for the Red Sox.

articles.title: 1B Jake Bauers, NLCS MVP with Brewers, reportedly agrees to 4-year, $58 million deal with Red Sox
articles.summary: Bauers, one of Milwaukee's heroes during its dominant World Series run, is headed to Boston, according to an ESPN report.
articles.body:
First baseman Jake Bauers, the reigning NLCS MVP , is reportedly headed to Boston after helping deliver the Milwaukee Brewers their first-ever World Series ring.

Bauers and the Red Sox have agreed to a four-year, $58 million deal, according to multiple reports on Friday .

Boston, which finished 23rd in MLB in runs per game this past season , will welcome the 31-year-old Bauers, who's coming off a career year.

His .389 on-base percentage was the second best among all NL players in 2026 . In addition to racking up a career-high 26 home runs and 86 RBI, he also ranked 10th in the majors with 94 walks drawn.

As a result of Bauers signing with the Red Sox for more than $50 million — and because the Brewers are revenue-sharing recipients — Milwaukee will get a compensatory draft pick between the end of the first round and Competitive Balance Round A, per ESPN .

After previously playing for Tampa Bay, Cleveland, Seattle and the New York Yankees, Bauers landed with the Brewers. He broke out this past season, his third with the club.

Not only did he lead Milwaukee in home runs during the regular season, but he also became one of its postseason heroes. During the NLCS, he slashed .286/.412/.571 with six RBI in a sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

In Game 2, he worked a 12-pitch walk against Dodgers righty Yoshinobu Yamamoto, setting the stage for Christian Yelich's go-ahead two-run single. In Game 3, he went yard off L.A. southpaw Blake Snell, launching a go-ahead, two-run homer on the 11th pitch of a seventh-inning at-bat. He went on to collect NCLS MVP honors.

The Brewers ultimately extended him a $23.15 million qualifying offer, which multiple executives expected him to accept, per ESPN's report . However, Bauers reportedly took the first long-term deal of his career.

Notably, in the immediate aftermath of Milwaukee defeating the Rays and winning it all last month, a camera captured Bauers handing the game-ending ball to Brewers manager Pat Murphy . Murphy hugged Bauers — among Yahoo Sports' top-10 free agents this offseason — and said the following:

"You're going to be a rich f***er. Just remember when you're on that horses*** Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourself, just remember this is the way we used to do it."

Bauers laughed off the remark, and Murphy, upon learning the moment went viral, said he called New York general manager Brian Cashman to clarify that he wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

Ironically, Bauers wound up with the Yankees' rivals.

Although the Red Sox have first baseman Willson Contreras, a four-time All-Star, under contract for one more season, Bauers can slot in at designated hitter.

articles.title: From journeyman to $58M: Jake Bauers heads to Boston in smart move for Red Sox
articles.summary: Bringing Bauers into the fold is a definitive upgrade. Kudos to Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow for acting quickly and decisively in a...
articles.body:
Sixteen days ago, first baseman Jake Bauers, blue and gold confetti beneath his cleats, gifted the World Series Game 5 final-out ball to Brewers manager Pat Murphy .

Clad head to toe in championship paraphernalia, the two embraced on the Tropicana Field turf. Murphy, always the provocateur, then prodded his pointer finger into Bauers' chest and delivered to the NLCS MVP an off-color near-truth.

"Just remember when you're on that horses*** Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourselves? Just remember, this is the way we used to do it."

Not exactly right, but far, far from wrong.

Bauers, 2026's most unexpected breakout offensive performer, reportedly agreed on a four-year, $58 million contract with the Boston Red Sox on Friday afternoon . ESPN's Jeff Passan first reported the news.

With free agency less than a fortnight old, the 31-year-old Bauers is now the highest-ranked free agent to agree to a new deal. Milwaukee extended to Bauers the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer, and there was significant industry speculation that he might accept. But the former journeyman — Bauers struggled for five different clubs before his Milwaukee ascension — found a sufficiently enticing bid on the open market.

Somewhere, Murphy is smiling and nodding.

For the Red Sox, Bauers is a logical, invigorating addition for a flawed, yet promising offensive unit. Boston managed just two runs total between two postseason drubbings against the Yankees in the AL's wild-card round. Injuries played a part in that lackluster showing, but even so, the Red Sox rolling with Jahmai Jones as the leadoff hitter in an elimination game was extremely telling.

The lineup was uninspiring all season. Boston ranked 19th in OPS, 23rd in runs per game and 26th in home runs. Young linchpin Roman Anthony missed 101 games with a finger issue. Trevor Story tallied just 266 plate appearances due to a sports hernia. Midseason trade acquisitions Adley Rutschman and Curtis Mead underwhelmed and got hurt, respectively. Jarren Duran was the second-worst qualified hitter in the sport by wRC+ and took 608 plate appearances.

Bauers' unique combo of patience and power could be exactly what this lineup needs. Boston ranked 24th in chase rate and 27th in hard-hit rate. Its newest slugger was elite in both categories. But while his offensive profile is a no-brainer, what exactly Bauers' arrival precipitates for preexisting personnel remains to be seen.

He'll likely split time with 2026 All-Star Willson Contreras at first base and DH. Bauers could also see time in the outfield; he spent 46 games there in 2026.

That means Anthony, who took a lot of DH reps in 2026, becomes the everyday option in left field. Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela, both of whom received down-ballot MVP votes, are entrenched in right and center.

It leaves Duran, who finished eighth in AL MVP two years ago, without a starting role. Barring injury elsewhere on the roster, he'll either be traded or move into a bench role. The same is true for Masataka Yoshida, who was again severely limited by injury. Triston Casas, a once-promising first baseman who finished third in AL Rookie of the Year voting in 2023, becomes an obvious change-of-scenery candidate.

However the positional cards fall, bringing Bauers into the fold is a definitive upgrade. Kudos to Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow for acting quickly and decisively in a unique market hurtling toward a lockout after Dec. 1.

For Bauers, the payday is well-earned. Drafted by the Padres in the seventh round of the 2013 MLB Draft, the Huntington Beach kid was dealt to the Rays about 18 months later in the three-team deal that made Trea Turner a National. Bauers reached The Show in 2018, but failed to gain a foothold with the Rays. They shipped him to Cleveland a year later in another three-team swap that brought Yandy Díaz to the Rays.

From there, Bauers stalled out. Too good for the minors, not dynamic enough for the bigs. He ended up on the Mariners, then spent time in Triple-A with Cincinnati, eventually ending up as an up-down bench bat for a bad 2023 Yankees team. Milwaukee took a flyer on Bauers that winter, adding the unproven lefty for a pair of low-level minor leaguers. He was a viable if unspectacular reserve option in 2024, but rejoined the Brewers the following season on only a minor league deal. Bauers took a step forward in 2025 with a scorching, portentous end to that campaign.

This past season, Bauers was squarely one of the league's best all-around hitters. He finished 11th in OPS, third in OBP and seventh in wRC+. The under-the-hood metrics were even better. Bauers was one of just two bats in baseball to finish in the top-10th percentile in hard-hit rate, launch-angle sweet spot rate and barrel percentage. The other was AL MVP Yordan Alvarez . Notably, Bauers ran a higher walk rate than the Houston slugger.

October offered a national stage for Bauers to showcase his glow-up. He delivered multiple double-digit show-stopping war-of-attrition plate appearances against the Dodgers in the NLCS. Both his seven-minute walk against Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 and series-altering big fly against Blake Snell in Game 3 will be remembered for generations among Wisconsin ball fans. Bauers also emerged as one of the spiritual leaders of a Brewers team that prided itself in a selfless, measured offensive approach.

"We came up with a plan offensively. The scoreboard isn't going to dictate it," he told Yahoo Sports after Milwaukee's comeback victory in World Series Game 2. "The focus is making sure everybody knows that it doesn't matter."

Bauers will now take that mentality to Boston, leaving a void in Milwaukee's championship lineup, though nobody doubts its ability to fill it.

They'll receive a compensatory draft pick after the first round.

articles.title: Brian Cashman Reveals Yankees' 'Main Priority' in MLB Free Agency Amid Latest Rumors
articles.summary: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman revealed that the team will be focused on making bullpen additions in free agency.
articles.body:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman revealed that the team will be focused on making bullpen additions in free agency.

"It's our main priority, to be honest," Cashman told MLB Network Radio on SiriusXM, via MLB.com's Bryan Hoch .

The Yankees' bullpen excelled during the 2026 season, ranking No. 2 among all teams with a 3.13 ERA. New York's relief pitchers also allowed just 484 total hits, the best mark in the American League.

Still, the Yankees could lose several relievers in free agency.

Left-hander Tim Hill and right-hander Paul Blackburn are both free agents. Closer David Bednar's long-term future in New York is also uncertain, although the team extended a qualifying offer to him on Nov. 2.

"Two of the three pitchers going into our eighth and ninth inning are gone; Blackburn and Bednar right now are free agents, so we've got our work to do," Cashman said, via Hoch. "And because of that, I am casting a wide net. We are asking around, and we need to find some stuff so we can feel good and sleep at night."

The Yankees are coming off a 93-68 finish last season, advancing to the ALDS before getting swept by the Tampa Bay Rays.

While it's worth noting that New York was without three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge throughout the playoffs due to a rib injury , the team still suffered its second consecutive ALDS exit following a World Series appearance in 2024.

As the Yankees look to go on a deeper postseason run and return to the Fall Classic next season, they're expected to address their bullpen in free agency.

Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander issued an apology on Friday for his anti-Islam posts on social media.

More than a week after sharing the posts on his Instagram story, the veteran used the same platform to publish a lengthy statement acknowledging the harm of his posts and affirming his respect for the Muslim community.

As a man of faith, it is my belief that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their religion, background, or beliefs. The posts were removed from Santander's IG story hours after they began receiving notice elsewhere.

"There really aren't words to express my level of disappointment with him making those comments. I've expressed that to him. I think anything exacerbating some level of anti-Islamic hate is just extremely concerning, extremely disappointing. I also talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant. "We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. His first season with the club in 2025 saw him play only 54 games due to a lingering shoulder injury and slash only .175/.271/.294. His injury worsened during the 2025 postseason and resulted in surgery on his left labrum .

Santander began a rehab assignment in September of this year, but played only five games before his season ended without a return to MLB. articles.title: Tigers 'Showing Interest' In Cubs Free Agent Who Gives Up A Ton Of Home Runs
articles.summary: The Detroit Tigers are looking at Shota Imanaga
articles.body:
The Detroit Tigers could use some more pitching, and according to MLB Network's Jon Morosi , they are "showing interest" in Shota Imanaga.

The Tigers traded away Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize at the trade deadline and Jack Flaherty is a free agent. The rotation will need some new arms, and Imanaga is an interesting case.

He is not one of the top arms on the market, but he does have a 3.45 ERA in 86 career starts with the Chicago Cubs. He had a 3.77 ERA last season and struck out 174 batters. Michael King and Freddy Peralta seem like better options, and the Tigers will surely check in on them as well.

While Imanaga does have an All-Star nod, he has one fatal flaw. He gives up a ton of home runs. He gave up 35 homers last season and 31 in 2025. Even during his All-Star season, he gave up 27 home runs. He has been top five in home runs allowed in each of his seasons as a big leaguer, and was second last season.

On a positive note, he does not walk a ton of batters. He ranked in the 95th percentile for walk rate last season.

Imanaga could perform better in Comerica Park. It is a tougher venue to hit home runs in than Wrigley Field, which could help solve some of his woes.

articles.title: Schlittler And Rice Earn Historic MVP Votes Despite Yankees’ Early Exit
articles.summary: Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice finish high in AL MVP voting. See how two Yankees stood out despite a disappointing season. Read the full breakdown now.
articles.body:
Even after a season that ended too soon for New York, two Yankees found their names at the top of the league's award lists. This result stands out because the team itself struggled to reach the final rounds of the playoffs. Yordan Alvarez took home the award with all 30 first-place votes, but the Yankees duo carved out their own space in the race.

One voter, Dave Skretta of the Associated Press, broke the pattern by casting a second-place vote for Schlittler. This choice put the pitcher just seven points behind Bobby Witt Jr. for third place. According to Pinstripe Alley , this fourth-place finish matches the best result for a pure pitcher since Shane Bieber in 2020. The last time a pitcher won the award in the National League was 2014.

Cam Schlittler's run to the All-MLB First Team as a starting pitcher was no accident. He posted an AL-best 1.95 ERA over 193.2 innings. This performance earned him the AL Cy Young Award as well. He became the third Yankee starter to receive an All-MLB selection since the league started the honor in 2019. The stats show he was the most reliable arm in the league, even if the team did not go far.

While the offense sputtered at times, Schlittler kept his team in games with steady pitching. His ability to limit runs over a full season set a new standard for the franchise. The fact that he received a second-place vote in the MVP race proves that voters saw his value beyond just wins and losses.

Ben Rice proved he could handle the pressure of the designated hitter role. The regular season saw him tally 41 home runs and 97 RBI. Being among the league's top hitters is demonstrated by his .897 OPS and 149 wRC+. According to Pinstripe Alley, Rice became the first Yankee DH to ever receive an All-MLB nod. He landed on the Second Team for his work at the plate.

Rice also shined when it mattered most. He hit four home runs in the 2026 postseason, which was the most by anyone in the playoffs. He received two third-place votes in the MVP voting, showing respect from the league's writers. His presence in the lineup added power to the Yankees during a tough year.

Despite the team's early exit, seven Yankees earned All-MLB nominations in total. Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Cody Bellinger were among those recognized. Bellinger even took home the Platinum Glove for his defensive work. Junior Caminero finished second in the MVP voting, missing only three second-place votes.

In the AL MVP race, only two Yankees got votes: Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice. According to Pinstripe Alley, the league has already recognized their contributions with these top honors.

articles.title: Clay Holmes Free Agency: Five Landing Spots For The Starter
articles.summary: Clay Holmes hits free agency after a solid season. Just Baseball breaks down five teams that could sign the 33-year-old starter.
articles.body:
Clay Holmes is back on the market, and the deal looks different this time. The former Yankees closer has successfully turned himself into a starting pitcher. After throwing 101 1/3 innings for the Chicago Cubs and New York Mets, he turned down his $12 million player option for 2027. A fractured right fibula stopped his season in May, but he returned in August to make nine starts for Chicago, according to Just Baseball . Beyond the top-tier names on the market, franchises now view him as a reliable rotation choice.

His numbers show a pitcher who limits damage rather than striking out everyone. Holmes posted a 3.29 ERA last season with a 3.63 FIP and a 1.19 WHIP. He gave up only six home runs in 101 1/3 innings. The 33-year-old relies on a sinker that accounts for nearly half his pitches. Just Baseball states that he induced groundballs on 60.8% of batted balls during the previous season. This skill set helps him limit hard contact even when his 18.6% strikeout rate stays low.

Just Baseball predicts Holmes will sign a three-year, $54 million deal with the New York Mets. That works out to an $18 million annual average value. Prior to 2025, he inked a three-year, $38 million deal with the Mets following years spent mostly in relief. New York gave him the chance to start again, a role he had not held regularly since his minor league days. He answered with 165 2/3 innings, a career high, alongside a 3.53 ERA in 31 starts. The Mets know his stuff, and they know he can handle the innings.

Other clubs might offer more money, but the fit is clear. Relying on his sinker to prevent batters from lifting the ball, Holmes extended his success into 2026. His changeup held opponents to a .186 average, while his sweeper allowed just a .154 batting average. Whether teams value his output against his injury record and age will determine his next contract. The Mets are the logical place for him to land again.

Just Baseball projects a contract length of two to four years with an expected annual average value between $16 million and $22 million. Holmes is 34 in 2027, so teams will be cautious about the long term. His 10.0% walk rate also means the defense behind him is crucial for his success. He needs fielders to turn groundballs into outs since he does not miss many bats. A team with a strong infield defense would be the perfect partner for his style.

The injury is the main worry. On May 15, Spencer Jones hit a 111.1 mph comebacker that broke Holmes's right fibula. The ailment removed him from action for almost three months and brought his time in Queens to a close. When the deadline arrived, the Cubs acquired Holmes and outfielder Tyrone Taylor from New York. Despite the setback, his ability to induce groundballs remains his greatest asset. Teams need to decide if the risk is worth the reward of a reliable innings eater.

Several teams need rotation help, and Just Baseball notes Holmes provides an option cheaper than the priciest starters. Before the injury occurred, the right-hander posted a 2.39 ERA over nine starts to begin 2026. His body of work proves he can handle a starter's workload when healthy. The New York Mets remain the top predicted landing spot for the free agent.

articles.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong Wins MVP With Historic 40/40 Season
articles.summary: Pete Crow-Armstrong becomes the first Cub to join the 40/40 club and wins NL MVP unanimously, beating out Shohei Ohtani in a historic night for Chicago.
articles.body:
Pete Crow-Armstrong became the first Chicago Cub to ever join the 40/40 club. He also won the National League MVP award with every single vote going to him. This result shocked many fans who expected a close race with Shohei Ohtani. The 24-year-old outfielder put together a season that will be talked about for decades. His numbers were so strong that the Baseball Writers' Association of America could not even split their vote.

Crow-Armstrong finished the year with a .280 batting average and a .570 slugging mark. He hit 45 home runs while stealing 41 bases to complete the rare feat. Bleed Cubbie Blue reported that he also led all of Major League Baseball in runs scored with 119. No other player in the league reached his level of total offense. He topped the National League in slugging percentage, OPS, and OPS+ while setting the bar for power and speed.

Chicago has waited a long time for a position player to win this honor. Crow-Armstrong is just the fourth Cub position player in history to post a season with a 9.8 bWAR or better. Fangraphs gave him an even higher mark of 10.6 fWAR for his work. He does not turn 25 until March, which means his best years are still ahead of him. This award marks the first time a Cub has won the MVP since Kris Bryant in 2016.

His patience at the plate grew massively compared to the year before. He walked 83 times, which is nearly three times the 29 walks he had in 2026. The rise in walks helped him drive in runs and get on base for his teammates. He hit 31 doubles and eight triples to add more damage to his game.

Crow-Armstrong has already climbed the career charts despite his young age. He has hit 86 home runs in his career, which ranks 35th on the Cubs all-time list. His 105 stolen bases also place him 32nd on the franchise record books. According to Bleed Cubbie Blue, he assembled one of the most remarkable single seasons in Cubs franchise history.

The unanimous vote sends a clear message about his dominance across the entire league. Every writer saw his value and agreed that no other player deserved the trophy more. This win cements his legacy as the face of the Chicago Cubs for years to come. Since Kris Bryant claimed the honor in 2016, no other Cub has won the award until Crow-Armstrong.

articles.title: Rangers Interest In Sato Faces $100M Price Tag Reality
articles.summary: The Rangers eye Teruaki Sato, but a nine-figure deal clashes with their payroll cap. Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon report the financial hurdles.
articles.body:
The Texas Rangers are looking at Teruaki Sato, but the price might be too high for this specific roster. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon note the club is pursuing the NPB star. They also note that Texas is a long shot given the expected cost. The Rangers have been focused on cutting costs rather than spending big on new free agents.

Sato is a left-handed hitter with massive power who just turned 28. This season, he produced 39 home runs with the Hashin Tigers, following a 40-home run campaign the prior year. His slash line was .306/.383/.609 across 614 plate appearances. MLB Trade Rumors predicted a five-year, $80 million deal, while other estimates put his value over $100 million. The signing team must also pay a posting fee based on the contract value.

The money is the biggest issue for a team that already pays too much. MLB Trade Rumors states the Rangers finished the 2026 season carrying a $192.8 million cash payroll. Their luxury tax number hit $218.7 million. They are projected to spend around $175 million in cash and $194 million on the tax next year. Chris Young, president of baseball operations, indicated payroll figures will remain comparable to this year's level.

Sato would likely need a contract in the nine-figure range. The Rangers have big obligations to Corey Seager, Jacob deGrom, and Nathan Eovaldi. They might not have the room to add another huge salary. The team could try to trade MacKenzie Gore or deal Jake Burger to create some short-term space. Even then, a nine-figure deal is a stretch for a team trying to balance the books.

There are other questions about where Sato would play. He has played mostly third base in Japan, but scouts think he projects more as a corner outfielder. The Rangers are set up nicely at third base with Josh Jung. They do have an opening at designated hitter since Joc Pederson is testing free agency. A left fielder might be acquired while Wyatt Langford continues playing center field.

Some teams worry about his hit tool translating to the majors. He struck out at a 26.7 percent rate in Japan, where the pitching is weaker than in Major League Baseball. Hitters from the NPB usually strike out more often when they come over. Sato likely faces a 30 percent strikeout rate upon playing in the US. That is a tradeoff teams make if he hits 30 or more homers.

The Rangers might be watching just in case the market collapses like it did for Munetaka Murakami a year ago. There is no harm in doing the scouting work without spending the money yet.

articles.title: Seattle Mariners Free Agency: Mariners May Have More Available Payroll Than Anticipated
articles.summary: According to recent comments from a team beat reporter, the Mariners may have more to spend this offseason than previously reported.
articles.body:
The Seattle Mariners front office concluded their time at the MLB general manager meetings Thursday in Las Vegas. The GM meetings yielded several updates on the Mariners' targets and goals this offseason.

Seattle will reportedly be targeting one of the top bats available on the open market this year, former Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki. The Mariners will attempt to host Suzuki in Seattle for an in-person visit before the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) expires Dec. 1 between the MLB and MLB Players Association and the lockout ensues.

In addition to Seattle's desire intention to land Suzuki, the team will also be looking to trade for a hitter to play the left side of the infield and will look to add multiple high-leverage relievers to the bullpen.

And it looks like that the Mariners will have more financial flexibility than initially thought to make that happen.

It was previously reported that Seattle's 2027 payroll would be what it ended 2026 with, roughly $170 million. Including projected arbitration numbers, that would leave the Mariners roughly $30-35 million available to spend in this abbreviated, one-month offseason.

However, the Mariners could have more to spend than that.

Seattle Times reporter Ryan Divish recently appeared on the Marine Layer podcast , where he stated that Seattle's 2027 payroll "should be" in the range of $175-$180 million.

That's not a huge jump from where the Mariners were originally thought to be going into next year, but it does bump up the team's estimated financial capability from $30-35 million to $40-45 million. And at extra $10-15 million could go a long way with this front office.

Suzuki has a market value of $27.5 million a year over a four-year deal per Spotrac .

If Suzuki is signed for his market value, that would mean that Seattle would have $12.5-17.5 million to spend for the rest of the offseason. Theoretically, that would be more than enough to land at least one available high-end reliever.

If the Mariners acquire an infielder and deal one of the highest-projected-earners in arbitration on the starting pitching rotation to get him, such as Logan Gilbert or George Kirby, that could clear up enough money to sign a second. Seattle could also attempt to land that second high-leverage reliever in a deal that includes that aforementioned infielder.

Suzuki is one of the best bats available, so the Mariners would likely have some competition to land him. Even with an extra $10 million available, a bidding war would likely place Seattle on the outside looking in, unless the team is determined to go against its free agent approach in the past.

Suzuki is an effective right-handed hitter, a plus-defender in the outfielder and could help the Mariners get back into the Japanese market, all of which are either areas of need or points of emphasis for the organization.

articles.title: This fact will only strengthen Giants legend Buster Posey’s Hall of Fame candidacy
articles.summary: The San Francisco Giants are yet to be good on the diamond with Buster Posey at the helm as the team’s president of baseball operations. But Posey has built...
articles.body:
The San Francisco Giants are yet to be good on the diamond with Buster Posey at the helm as the team's president of baseball operations. But Posey has built so much goodwill with both the Giants franchise and its fanbase after he spent the entirety of his illustrious career with the team that he has certainly earned the benefit of the doubt as he gains more and more experience in his executive career.

Posey will be eligible for the Hall of Fame as a member of the 2027 class. He spent 13 years with the Giants, won three World Series titles with them (2010, 2012, and 2014), and emerged as a legitimate leader that the entire locker room looked up to.

The intangible impact he had on the Giants franchise is unmistakable. He was elite behind the dish and called games for pitchers at such a high level that pitchers, like Jake Peavy, credit him for getting the best out of them. In an appearance on MLB Network, Peavy praised Posey for making the game easy for him to the point where he recorded an ERA of 2.17 in 12 appearances after San Francisco acquired him at the trade deadline.

"It's because [Buster Posey] was calling the pitches," Peavy said.

Prior to the trade, Peavy had a 4.72 ERA on the season in 20 games with the Boston Red Sox. He was already 33 at the time, so some decline was understandable, but he got a new lease in life with the Giants and helped them win their third World Series title in five years.

Peavy would only have two seasons left in the big leagues, but for a good stretch, he turned back the clock thanks in large part to his partnership with Posey.

Posey does not have the most eye-popping counting stats. He only had 158 home runs and 729 runs batted in for his career, although he did finish with a batting average of .302. But the Giants would not have won big without him, and the impact he had that stats could not account for must not go unnoticed.
